title: Quantum teleportation over a field-deployed hollow-core fibre network
authors: Ri-Yao Song, Ya-Zhou Zhao, Yun-Ru Fan, Yang-Bin Ma, Yan-Yu Wei, Si Shen, Hao Li, Li-Xing You, Kai Guo, Guang-Can Guo, Qiang Zhou
abstract: When a photon and one member of an entangled photon pair are jointly projected onto a Bell-state measurement (BSM), the quantum state of the photon can be transferred to the distant partner of the pair without physically transmitting this information carrier. In real-world deployment, however, teleportation performance is fundamentally bottlenecked by quantum channel impairments, such as loss, noise, and fluctuations, which induce severe decoherence and degrade fidelity. This vulnerability is further exacerbated in scenarios with intense classical data traffic or background light. Realizing scalable quantum networks, therefore, hinges on developing advanced channel architectures capable of supporting both high-fidelity quantum operations and high-capacity classical communications within a shared infrastructure. Towards this end, hollow core fibre (HCF) offers a promising quantum channel resource by combining free-space-like weak light-matter interaction with the stability of fibre-based systems. Here, utilizing a field-deployed metropolitan HCF network spanning three spatially separated nodes in Chengdu, we achieve quantum teleportation with an intermediate BSM under co-propagating classical traffic. Crucially, the HCF links preserve the long-term indistinguishability of photonic qubits without active stabilization, and exhibit a Raman noise approximately three orders of magnitude lower than that of standard solid-core counterparts. This noise suppression enables robust quantum teleportation even alongside classical launch powers up to 160 mW. Our findings establish a classical-data-compatible framework for quantum networking over deployed fibre infrastructure and offer a wavelength-agnostic, plug-and-play, and free-running pathway toward the quantum internet.
summary: This paper demonstrates quantum teleportation over a metropolitan network built using Hollow-Core Fibre (HCF). By showing that HCF drastically reduces noise compared to standard fibers, the authors establish a robust framework for coexisting quantum and classical data streams. This paves a practical path toward realizing scalable, field-deployable quantum internet infrastructure.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving high-fidelity quantum teleportation over real-world, deployed fiber optic networks while simultaneously coexisting with intense classical data traffic.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated robust quantum teleportation using a field-deployed Hollow-Core Fibre (HCF) network, showing that HCF significantly suppresses noise compared to solid-core fibers.
method: They implemented the quantum teleportation protocol using time-bin qubits and Bell-State Measurement (BSM), characterizing performance under high classical power levels up to 160 mW.
model_or_system: The experiment utilizes a metropolitan HCF network connecting three nodes. The system involves generating entangled pairs, performing BSM at an intermediate node, and transmitting quantum states over the deployed fiber infrastructure.
key_observables: Three-fold coincidence rates, teleportation fidelities ($\langle F^{(1)}angle$), Raman scattering coefficients (HCF vs. SCF), and polarization/HOM interference stability over time.
important_parameters: Classical launch powers up to 160 mW; noise suppression factor of approximately three orders of magnitude compared to standard fibers.
main_assumptions: The success relies on the HCF's ability to maintain long-term indistinguishability and exhibit significantly lower Raman noise, enabling a classical-data-compatible framework.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the deployed network topology in Chengdu, experimental setups detailing qubit generation and BSM integration with DWDM classical channels, and characterization plots comparing Raman scattering coefficients between HCF and SCF.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical setup (HCF deployment), the quantum protocol implementation (teleportation via BSM), rigorous performance testing under noise/classical load, and comparison of results against theoretical limits.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial experimental blueprint for scaling quantum networks by solving the critical engineering problem of integrating fragile quantum signals with high-power classical communication channels using novel fiber platforms like HCF.
